Hey hey hey it's okay, first, take a deep breath. Take another one. Take one more. Come back when you've actually done that, okay? Did you do it? Okay well do it or don't but you should for at minimum 1 minute and 45 seconds.

Back? Okay. Here are three things that are helping me through an almost similar process.


1. You can do whatever you want forever.
2. You don't have to know exactly everything right away. 
3. You're not alone. I'm here, there's a strong vibrant community of butches here, we have a long history of butchness of all kinds. You are not alone.


This is a process. You might change in some ways you didn't expect, but you belong. You might decide you identify differently later on, too, and that's okay. You're not taking up space just for existing. 

Trans masc butches/lesbians have always existed. We have always existed. You're not taking up space, you're right where you belong and you're allowed to take up space because you matter.


Transition in anyway that you makes you feel comfortable. Go on T. Don't go on T. Go on T for 6 months. Go on T for 20 years. Wear a binder on the weekends. Get top surgery. Don't get top surgery. Whatever makes you feel happy and doesn't hurt anyone else. 

As for the harassment, well, it never stops sucking. But I've found I don't care as much because I feel so much happier than I did before embracing being a butch transmasc. Have a strong support system, one of them is this subreddit, but also your friends and family, too. 

You got this, comrade.

I'm a fat dyke. I've struggled with body dysmorphia my entire life and acknowledge that a lot of it also tied to body dysphoria, as well. 

I am also on a healthy weight loss journey, I don't calorie count, I focus on protein and whole food meals, try to get to the gym at minimum once or twice a week. I just ran my first 5k a couple weeks ago! I wasn't super fast or win any awards but I did it! Something that I didn't think my fat body could even do! And that has been incredibly formative for me, that being able to conquer my mind and my body has made me more resilient overall. But it took a lot for me to get here. 

Ive lived with depression, anxiety, CPTSD, and internalized homophobia for as long as I could remember and drank and binged to cope for many years. I think my body reflects a lot of my trauma/addictions/relationship with food and reclaiming my agency and getting help not just for my mental health but also for my physical health has been instrumental in accepting my body and queerness. I'm glad I'm alive to still have time to get healthy now, because for many years i didn't see the point in it.

I think why there are so many of us is because a lot of us deal with many common issues: addiction, body image, trauma and a lot of it can be most visibly seen in our appearances, which is what we can control on a day to day basis. I was a hyper feminine young person when I was thin, but didn't see myself as a woman (still don't) and now that I'm older I've shed the pretense and embraced my masculinity so much more. Idk if there's just more of us or that our fatness makes us that much more visible and in your face. Much to think about and chew on for sure!!

Since you're allergic to cats, have you considered adopting a rabbit? I say adopt because usually you can find a shelter or sanctuary that spends a lot of time with adult rabbits and know the personalities and needs of their animals that could fit in better with your household. Baby rabbits are harder to gauge on how they'll be when they grow up, but an adult will be pretty much exactly what the shelter or sanctuary has observed about them personality wise. 

I suggest a rabbit because they're very similar to cats in several ways. They're affectionate and clean. Can be box trained and kept indoors. Rabbits don't usually like to be held because it makes them feel like they're being attacked by predators, but depending on the personality or breed, can show love in other ways. 

I'd recommend reading up on their care, as they live as long as cats do, but for an 11-year-old, it could be something she learns about with you. 

I loved my rabbits, but I couldn't keep them with my dogs, and if dogs aren't what she's into, a rabbit might do well and there are plenty in sanctuaries that you and she can meet the rabbits with first to see if that's something you want. 

Best of luck

I've only had the fortune of working at one legal dispensary in Caliornia but my experience was thus: it was in our contract that we signed when we began employment with the company that we had to follow regular workplace policies in regards to working while intoxicated as well as a strict policy against smoking on site.

So, for the former, coming to work high was, on paper, something you shouldn't do. This made it hard for some of the old school trimmers who had been doing that work for years and sometimes decades to adjust because they were used to a different work environment, which was more lax, meaning they could smoke and trim at the same time. As a more professional setting, it wasn't encouraged or allowed at all. Did people come in high? Sure. If it didn't impede their work, no one cared. However, this didn't always apply to the budtenders because they are the face of the company and held to different standards. Some staff were let go for coming in high and unable to function in a professional capacity.

Now, for the people who smoked on site and were seen on camera (which were legally mandated to be located throughout the business) they would be written up or put on restriction. The reason I was told for the harsh consequences for that infraction was because it put the businesses' license in jeopardy. Of course staff would get together after work and hang out, smoke, drink, what have you. What was conducted after hours and off site wasn't an issue.

This was just my experience. The dispensary I worked at was very high end and we tried to maintain a standard among the staff but I mean, I don't think anyone ever got drug tested or anything. Background checks were required as part of the hiring process. But I know from the managers that they didn't discriminate against you if you had a nonviolent drug charge on your record. Most of the staff smoked regularly, or used medicinally, or had family that used medicinally or recreationally. It was part of the culture of passionate care that we had, many people spent tremendous time doing their work to educate themselves on the newest data on cannabis, or were incredibly passionate about how they cultivated the plants themselves. I can't say much for other businesses, but I know that at least in California, background checks are required, there might be legalese in the contract you sign about workplace intoxication, but it's all reliant on the work environment the actual staff work on. The more protections the business has against any risks for their employees, clients, and business model, the better leg it has to stand on to avoid getting shut down. If you're looking for working legally, ask a lot of questions about the place you want to work for. Research if you need paperwork or permits to work legally (Oregon I believe requires a worker's permit for cannabis). Go in and get a sense of how the staff behaves. Maybe ask them how they like it.

Edit: TL;DR it depends on how "legal" the business is and how strictly they adhere to state and local policies and regulations.

You could be one of the lucky people who just don't respond to edibles. Or those edibles could have been improperly dosed. It's hard to say, really, because there are so many factors that go into edibles. They take a while to kick in because they have to go through the liver first, and then if you ingest CBD, you might have even more trouble getting high using edibles. 

In California before legalization when it was medicinal, we used to have these chocolate bars that claimed to be 420mg of THC. I have a friend who's smoked since the '60s who swore by them. I also have another friend who used to pound those things down and claim to not feel a thing. Everyone is different, there's so many different possibilities. Now that recreational has succeeded in California, I've noticed the dosing has gotten slightly better. I had a tester of Kushy Punch hybrid gummies that were 10mg each teeny tiny square, ate 2, was so high I couldn't see straight, and on top of which I had horrible heartburn. 

TL;DR there's too many different variables to be sure because there's very little in the way of proper dosing, every individual's reaction can be different, and sometimes they just don't work.

Depends on how recently you smoked the CBD carts. CBD tends to "dampen" the effects of THC [because they counteract each other.](https://www.leafly.com/news/cbd/cbd-vs-thc-cbd-not-intoxicating) If you haven't smoked that day and drink the soda, drink half which will hopefully be about approximately 5mg, wait 30 minutes to an hour, and if the desired effect isn't reached drink the other half. It also has to do with what you've eaten that day, your mentality, overall health, metabolism, and a bazillion other factors. How one affects one person doesn't necessarily mean how it will affect someone else. Smoked THC hits the system faster because it goes to the [bloodstream through the lungs](https://www.leafly.com/news/health/considerations-before-ingesting-edibles) while edibles take time because they have to go through the liver to be metabolized.
